newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean garment-maker seeks white knight over bid.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean garment-maker seeks white knight over bid.

text.p: New Star Trading Co said on Friday it was seeking a white knight to thwart a takeover bid by Savoy Hotel and avoid becoming South Korea's first listed company acquired in a hostile takeover.

New Star's plan followed the announcement earlier on Friday by Seoul-based Savoy Hotel that it would make a grab for the garment manufacturer by aiming for a 51 percent stake. A hotel official said Savoy would soon apply for tender offers.
But Kim Hong-kun, president of New Star Trading, said the company was safe from any hostile takeover bid and would make every effort to defend itself.
"We are now considering tender offers to counter Savoy's bid. And we are also seeking a white knight to ward off the predator," Kim told reporters.
A white knight is a potential friendly acquirer sought out by a company to protect itself from a hostile takeover.

"I'm very optimistic we will be able to secure more than a 50 percent stake in our company, taking into account the 40 percent stake friendly to us and the additional five percent from a buy-back scheme," Kim said.
He did not elaborate on the friendly 40 percent stake.
New Star said on Friday it would buy back five percent of its own common shares between April 21 and July 20.
"The buy-back decision is aimed at protecting our management from a corporate raider," Kim Hong-gil, an executive of New Star, said by telephone.
The company earlier offered a one-for-100 bonus issue on May 2 to try to raise the existing owner's stake and to seek a chance to analyse the shareholding structure.
Savoy startled the Seoul stock market when it told the bourse on Tuesday the hotel had raised its New Star holding to 24.7 percent from 13.59 percent in the open market.
It said it would buy an additional 26.3 percent stake soon but no date has been set.
"We plan to diversify business lines by acquiring the garment maker," said a Savoy Hotel official.
He said the hotel wanted to buy the additional shares at between 40,000 won ($44.77) and 50,000 won against 38,000 won which they paid for the 24.70 percent stake.
New Star's share price soared on news of the takeover bid. It hit a 1997 high of 66,500 won on Friday, skyrocketting from its year low of 18,700.
"We are waiting for the share price to fall," said the hotel official.
At present, the family of New Star's chairman and the company's affiliates hold a combined 29.26 percent stake, slightly outpacing Savoy's shareholding.
"Investors believe they can make profits from the fight between Savoy Hotel and New Star Trading," said Ha Sung-won of Ssangyong Securities.
But analysts said they believed the hotel wanted to reap profits from the rocketing share price rather than actually managing the company.
"I doubt if the hotel really has an interest in managing New Star Trading, which has no business link at all between the two," said a LG Securities analyst.
"Savoy seeks greenmail. I'm sure the hotel will not buy our shares through tender offers," New Star's Kim said.

Greenmail is a payment by a takeover target to a potential acquirer, usually to buy back acquired shares at a premium. In exchange, the acquirer agrees not to pursue the takeover bid. ($1 = 893.40 won)
